rows.summary: Refund the buyer the full $48.00 now. Your own order system shows the tote was never shipped because it was out of stock, so there is nothing to contest, and settling at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Message the buyer with the tracking number and ask them to allow a few more days for delivery. Tracking shows the tote shipped but not yet delivered, which is not enough to contest, and the case is still an early inquiry.

Refund the buyer the full 48.00 USD. The only tracking on file is cancelled, so you have no proof of delivery and a contest would almost certainly fail. Settling now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and the dispute fee.

The buyer opened this inquiry on Oct 3, the day before your USPS scan shows delivery to their San Jose address on Oct 4, so they likely received the tote after complaining. Message them with the tracking number and delivery details and ask them to check and close the case. If they don't respond, submit the USPS tracking as proof of fulfillment, ideally an official USPS tracking page, since PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED.

Message the buyer now rather than contesting. The only delivery proof is a merchant-entered scan whose ZIP (10001) doesn't match the ship-to ZIP (95131), and PayPal's tracker only shows SHIPPED. Verify the tracking directly on USPS.com first; if it confirms delivery to 95131, provide that as evidence, and if not, offer or refund before this escalates.

Don't contest yet: the only delivery scan (Sep 28) is dated before the buyer paid (Oct 2), so it likely belongs to a different shipment, and PayPal's tracker shows only SHIPPED. Message the buyer with the tracking number while you check the number with USPS; if it doesn't show delivery to this address after Oct 2, offer a refund or reship.

You've already submitted tracking and offered $20, and PayPal is waiting on the buyer, so send a short follow-up and wait for their reply. Note that PayPal's tracker shows the package only as SHIPPED, not delivered, so your contest position is weaker than it looks; consider confirming delivery directly with USPS.
Refund the $48.00 in full. The only tracking on file was cancelled, so there is no proof of delivery to win an item-not-received case, and a partial offer isn't an available option at this stage.

PayPal currently allows no actions on this $48.00 item-not-received case, which is under review, so there is nothing to submit right now. Outside PayPal, gather carrier tracking for the tote shipment to the San Jose address so it's ready if PayPal requests a response.

Submit supporting information showing delivery: the USPS record says the tote was delivered to the buyer's San Jose 95131 address on Oct 4, and the sale is eligible for seller protection. Attach the official USPS tracking page or screenshot, since PayPal's own tracker still shows only SHIPPED and the delivery scan on file was entered by you.

Refund the $8.00 in full. There is no tracking to prove delivery, and your shipping record (a vinyl sticker, order #3310) does not match the item on the PayPal order (a canvas tote), so you have nothing persuasive to contest with. Settling now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and any dispute fee.

The buyer has said they found the tote at a neighbor's and would close the case, but it is still open four days later. Send a short, friendly reminder asking them to close it; there's no need to refund or contest yet.

Submit proof of fulfillment: the merchant-entered USPS scan shows this $900 tote was delivered on Oct 5 with an adult signature by J DOE in San Jose 95131, which matches the buyer's ship-to address. Attach the official USPS tracking and signature record, since PayPal's own tracker still shows only SHIPPED.

Contest with proof of fulfillment: USPS tracking shows the tote was delivered to the buyer's ship-to ZIP, and the buyer agrees it was delivered. Under seller protection, a porch theft after confirmed delivery is generally not the seller's liability. Upload the official USPS tracking page, since PayPal's own tracker still shows only SHIPPED.

Message the buyer while you check your shipping records. PayPal has no tracking on file, so contesting now would fail. If you have carrier tracking showing delivery to the San Jose address, submit it as evidence. If the tote never shipped or can't be traced, refund the full $300 before the case escalates.

Message the buyer with the tracking number and ask them to check again; it shipped, but there is no delivery confirmation yet. Messaging is the only action PayPal allows at this inquiry stage, and settling now avoids escalation to a claim.

Submit proof of fulfillment: USPS shows the tote was delivered to the buyer's San Jose address on Oct 4, and the sale is eligible for seller protection. The buyer already rejected your $15 offer, so a further partial refund is unlikely to settle this. Include the carrier's own tracking page, because PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED.

Contest with proof of fulfillment. The buyer confirms the box arrived, the delivery scan places it at the shipping address, and the packed weight (1.8 lb) matches the label weight, which suggests the box was not empty. Attach the official USPS tracking page and label receipt rather than a hand-entered scan, because the PayPal tracker still only shows SHIPPED.

Refund the full $30.00 now. The buyer's photo shows the mug cracked through the handle, which makes a partial refund unlikely to satisfy them, and settling at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Message the buyer with your listing and packing photo showing the tote is olive green, and ask whether they'd like to return it or would accept a small goodwill refund. The color complaint is subjective, so a friendly reply at this early inquiry stage is the cheapest way to settle before it escalates.

Offer a 25.00 USD partial refund for the missing tote. Your own packing log confirms only one of the two totes was packed, so contesting would fail, and settling now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Reply to the buyer with the item's serial number and authenticity certificate, and ask what makes them think it is fake. The case is still an inquiry and the buyer's only complaint is a three-word note, so a clear reply may resolve it before escalation.

Submit proof of fulfillment: the transaction is eligible for seller protection, and the tracking you added shows the tote delivered to the San Jose ship-to address on the order. Attach the official USPS tracking record rather than relying only on your own note.

Refund the $15.00 in full. This is an unauthorised-transaction case on a digital download that is not eligible for seller protection, and there is no evidence on file that would persuade PayPal, so settling now at the inquiry stage is the cheapest way to close it before escalation.

Your refund log shows a full 48.00 USD PayPal refund (ID 6RT43210AB987654C) issued on 2026-10-03, the same day the buyer wrote. Submit that refund record as proof of refund rather than refunding again, which would pay the buyer twice.

Accept the claim and refund the 48.00 USD. Your own order system shows the buyer was charged twice for one shipped tote, so this duplicate-charge inquiry is valid. Settling now at the inquiry stage avoids escalation and PayPal's dispute fee.

Submit proof of fulfillment: the USPS scan shows the tote was delivered to the buyer's San Jose ZIP on Oct 4, the day after the buyer messaged. Attach the official USPS tracking page, because PayPal's tracker still only shows SHIPPED.

Refund the buyer the full 48.00 USD. Your returns log shows a return received with no refund issued, so contesting would fail. First confirm that return #2290 is this order, because the log date matches the payment date.

Contest this item-not-received inquiry with proof of fulfillment: the USPS tracking number is on file with PayPal, and the delivery scan shows the tote was delivered to the buyer's San Jose 95131 address on Oct 4. The note in your order asking for an immediate refund is not a reason to refund, and you are seller-protection eligible.

Contest with proof of fulfillment: USPS shows the $48 tote delivered on Oct 4 to the buyer's San Jose 95131 address, and the sale qualifies for seller protection. Attach the official USPS tracking page, since PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED and the delivery scan was entered by you.

Submit proof of fulfillment. USPS shows the tote was delivered on Oct 4 to the buyer's San Jose address, the day after the buyer opened this not-received case. Attach the official USPS tracking page or screenshot, because PayPal's tracker still shows only SHIPPED.

PayPal currently allows no actions on this $48.00 item-not-received inquiry, so take no action on PayPal for now. Outside PayPal, find the carrier tracking for the tote shipped to San Jose, and check whether it shows delivery, so you are ready to respond when PayPal opens a response.

Message the buyer to ask for photos of the canvas tote. The order was for a canvas tote, but their photo shows a cracked ceramic mug, so the claim doesn't match what was sold. At the inquiry stage, a polite request for clarification costs nothing and may settle the case or build your record before you consider contesting.

Don't make an offer yet. The tote appears to have been delivered to the buyer's ZIP code, and PayPal's only option right now is a refund offer. Contact the buyer outside PayPal with the tracking details, and be ready to contest with USPS delivery proof if this becomes a claim.

Message the buyer that the order shipped with tracking and you are checking with the carrier. Don't contest yet, because tracking shows only SHIPPED, not delivered. Don't refund $1,200 yet either, since the order was paid only a week ago and the case is still an inquiry.
